description: We’re Recycllux, a team that loves building, exploring new technologies, and solving real-world problems. For Dancing with the SARs, we want to turn satellite data into something useful, visual, and easy to understand. We’re looking for curious teammates interested in Earth science, SAR/GIS, AI/ML, web development, UI/UX, or design. Our idea is still evolving, so bring your skills, ideas, and creativity! 🚀🌍
summary:
RiverNexa is a river-intelligence platform that combines NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar observations, hydrological data and, in its next development phase, local PelaNode probe measurements to reveal how river and wetland systems are changing.

For the 2026 Danube low-water crisis, we built an interactive application using real NISAR L2 GCOV data to map open water and water beneath dense vegetation across the Danube Delta and other Lower Danube locations. Our preliminary analysis showed that visible open water remained comparatively stable while the NISAR-derived flooded-vegetation class declined sharply during summer 2026.
RiverNexa addresses the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge by turning repeated NISAR observations into an interpretable time-series of hydrological change. 

RiverNexa is designed to combine space, field and contextual data so authorities and water users can identify where conditions are changing, prioritise inspections and make better-informed decisions.
details:
The challenge:
The Danube experienced severe low-water conditions during 2026, affecting ecosystems, agriculture, navigation, energy and water-dependent communities. Traditional monitoring is essential but fragmented. River gauges provide highly accurate water-level and discharge measurements at fixed points. Optical satellites provide intuitive maps of visible surface water, but clouds and dense vegetation can obscure important wetland hydrology. Field measurements provide high-value local information, but they are sparse in space and time. Discharge at Baziaș fell to about 1,500 m³/s in August 2026, against a multiannual August average of about 3,900 m³/s (a drop of roughly 60%). Low water forced both reactors at the Cernavodă nuclear plant offline (Unit 1 on 28 July, Unit 2 on 13 August 2026). The Romanian government put the three-month loss at about EUR 200 million.

RiverNexa was developed to address this monitoring gap.

Our central question was: Can NISAR reveal hydrological change across river corridors and vegetated wetlands that is difficult to observe using conventional monitoring alone, and can that information ultimately be combined with field sensing to support better river-management decisions?

 

What we developed:

RiverNexa is an interactive river-intelligence platform built around three complementary data streams: NASA–ISRO NISAR observations, PelaNode in-situ sensing and contextual hydrological data.

NASA NISAR. NISAR provides the wide-area satellite view. We process real NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV L-band radar scenes over the Lower Danube and Danube Delta to identify changes in open water, wetland inundation, water beneath dense vegetation, river and floodplain surface conditions, and hydrological change through time. L-band radar is particularly valuable for RiverNexa because it can provide information in cloudy conditions and can respond to water beneath vertical vegetation such as reeds. NISAR’s L-band radar has a 24 cm wavelength and a 242 km swath, and it images nearly all land surfaces twice every 12 days, giving the repeat coverage needed for time-series of change (NASA/JPL).

PelaNode. PelaNode is the planned in-situ data stream. The current hackathon prototype does not yet ingest live PelaNode measurements. The next development phase will connect field probes to RiverNexa alongside NISAR. Candidate field measurements include water level or stage at the deployment point, temperature, conductivity or salinity, and dissolved oxygen. These measurements provide local, high-frequency information that satellite observations alone cannot provide.

NISAR provides the wide-area space signal. PelaNode provides the local field signal. RiverNexa combines both.

Contextual hydrological data.  RiverNexa can also incorporate contextual information such as river gauges, river discharge, weather, land cover, management information and historical conditions.

The long-term architecture is: NISAR + PelaNode + contextual data → RiverNexa → river intelligence → decisions.

 

What RiverNexa does:

RiverNexa is designed to fuse different evidence streams, detect where hydrological conditions are changing, compare present conditions with previous observations, prioritise areas where attention or field investigation is most important, alert users to significant changes, and support decisions by authorities, environmental managers and water users.

The system does not automatically make regulatory or operational decisions. It provides evidence to help responsible users decide where to investigate and act.

 

What we found:

Our preliminary NISAR analysis of the Danube Delta revealed a striking contrast. Between 18 June and 16 October 2026, our team-derived reed-bed water class (NISAR HH double-bounce backscatter) declined from approximately 837 km² to 104 km² (-88%), while the visible open-water area rose slightly from 1,091 km² to 1,124 km². This does not mean that the Delta literally “lost 733 km² of water.” It means that the radar-derived class associated with inundated vegetation changed dramatically. This distinction is scientifically important. The result suggests that visible open-water maps alone may not reveal the full hydrological condition of a wetland.

 

Validation and scientific uncertainty:

We treated scientific validity as a central part of the project. The open-water component of the analysis was compared against independent satellite observations. Our project work also compared temporal behaviour across independent NISAR tracks and against hydrological discharge information.

However, we deliberately distinguish between observed or derived results and hypotheses requiring further validation. For example, the strong relationship observed between our wetland signal and Danube discharge is an association, not proof that drought alone caused the entire change. Vegetation seasonality may also influence the radar response. Direct field measurements beneath the reeds are therefore an important next step.

 

Why NISAR is essential:

NASA data is not an additional visualization layer in RiverNexa. It is the central analytical input.

Without NISAR, RiverNexa would still have river gauges, optical imagery and field measurements, but it would lose the wide-area L-band radar signal that allows us to investigate hydrological change across vegetated wetlands and floodplains.

We use NISAR L2 GCOV data, not a ready-made wetland product. The RiverNexa team processes the radar observations and derives the change information shown in the application.

 

Why the project is creative:

RiverNexa's innovation lies in the integration of Earth observation, local field sensing, hydrological context and decision intelligence.

Existing tools frequently operate independently. A river gauge measures one location. A satellite observes a large area. A field probe measures local conditions.

RiverNexa is designed to bring these evidence streams together in one operational view. The goal is not to replace existing monitoring systems, but to connect them.

 

Intended users: 

Potential RiverNexa users include water and basin authorities, wetland and protected-area managers, municipalities and regional authorities, aquaculture operators and fisheries managers, restoration programmes, and climate-adaptation and resilience organisations.

Different users require different decisions. A wetland manager may ask: Where is hydrological stress emerging and where should we inspect first? A fish farm may ask: Where might local oxygen or temperature stress require attention? A water authority may ask: Where is low river flow producing the strongest ecological response?

RiverNexa is designed to turn multiple measurements into evidence for these decisions.

 

Impact:

The Danube basin supports more than 80 million people across 19 countries. The 2026 drought demonstrated that water stress is not only an environmental issue. It can affect ecosystems, agriculture, fisheries and aquaculture, inland navigation, energy infrastructure, water availability and local economies. The Danube River Basin covers about 801,000 km² (ICPDR). At Lake Srebarna in Bulgaria, low water stopped Dalmatian pelican nesting in summer 2026, and emergency pumping moved more than 5 million m³ of Danube water into the lake over 74 days (Bulgarian Ministry of Environment and Water; BTA).

RiverNexa cannot stop drought. Its potential impact is to help users understand changing conditions earlier, identify where investigation is most valuable and reduce the time between observation and action.

The Danube is the first demonstrator, but the architecture is designed to be transferable to other rivers, floodplains and vegetated wetlands where NISAR coverage and local validation are available.

 

Technologies and resources:

The RiverNexa prototype uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV L-band radar data, satellite and hydrological contextual datasets, a web-based interactive visualization environment, 3D geospatial visualization, radar image processing and time-series analysis, automated and AI-assisted processing components, and future PelaNode in-situ sensing integration.

The application distinguishes between real observations, simulated workflow components and future functionality so users can understand the maturity of each part of the system.

 

Current maturity:

Working now: The current prototype already supports NISAR data access and processing, Lower Danube and Danube Delta visualization, multi-date hydrological-change analysis, an interactive web interface, river-level and hydrological context, and preliminary wetland-change analysis.

In development: The next development stage includes live PelaNode data ingestion, satellite-probe data fusion, calibrated decision thresholds, automated alerting and field validation.

Next phase: We intend to deploy PelaNode probes at selected sites and build the first paired satellite and field dataset. This will allow us to test how NISAR signals relate to local water conditions, how seasonality affects interpretation, whether combined satellite and probe information can provide useful decision lead time, and whether the architecture transfers successfully to other river and wetland systems.
